plot_extraction.response_text:
William receives a shilling from his aunt and spends half on cheap green sweets and half on an afternoon at the cinema. Enthralled by films about criminals, romance, comedy, and a drunkard’s tragic child, he spends the rest of the day imitating their plots.

Pretending to flee imaginary pursuers, William charges into his father, who angrily throws his sweets into the garden. After recovering the now-dirty sweets, William shares them with Joan next door. Inspired by a romantic film, he adopts a husky, dramatic voice; when Joan assumes he is seriously ill, he encourages her belief that he has weak lungs. The sweets make her sick, and her mother later contacts William’s bewildered family.

William next misinterprets a conversation between his sister Ethel and Jack Morgan. Believing they secretly love each other but are too proud to admit it, he visits Jack, gives him a crushed rosebud supposedly from Ethel, claims she is wasting away with love, and summons him to a private meeting at seven. Jack arrives during the family’s dinner hour, causing an awkward interview with a mortified Ethel.

Finally, copying a painter he saw in a comedy, William uses a flame and penknife to strip paint from his bedroom door. His already irritable father punishes him and declares him insane, while William regards all the resulting disasters as unfair misunderstandings. Remembering the film about the drunkard and his forgiving child, William casts himself as the tragic victim and begins offering his father melodramatic forgiveness before wisely fleeing.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is a comic domestic adventure told by an assured third-person narrator who stays close to William’s point of view while retaining an adult awareness of his mistakes. This dual perspective is central to the style: William’s fantasies and deductions are presented with enough sympathy to seem internally reasonable, but the narrator’s dry phrasing exposes their absurdity. The tone is affectionate rather than cruel. William is troublesome, self-dramatising and opportunistic, yet his imaginative energy makes him more appealing than the exasperated adults who judge only the resulting chaos.

The humour relies heavily on irony, incongruity and escalation. Elevated language is repeatedly applied to trivial childish concerns: choosing cheap sweets requires “deep calculations,” shopkeepers are judged through a rigorous system of patronage and boycott, and a dirty bag of confectionery becomes a precious possession. Mock-heroic comparisons, such as William adopting “the air of a Rothschild,” magnify his self-importance. Comic effects also arise from the gap between intention and consequence. William believes he is behaving like a pursued criminal, a rustic lover, a stoical invalid, a romantic mediator and a scientific experimenter; everyone else sees assault, illness, improper interference and vandalism. Each new misunderstanding grows naturally out of something he has watched at the cinema, giving the episode a tightly linked chain of cause and effect.

The narrator’s irony is often compressed into balanced, deadpan statements. Sentences such as the observation that William consumed sweets and garden soil “in fairly equal proportions” report absurdity with formal calm. Similar understatement governs the parodies of the films. Their clichés are anatomised through precise, exaggerated description: criminals behave in ways “guaranteed to attract attention,” a villain is identified by his moustache, emotions demand “gymnastic skill,” and melodramatic suffering becomes so energetic that a relapse is scarcely surprising. Repetition intensifies the satire, especially in phrases like “simple country maiden” and “simple country son of the soil.” The prose thus mocks early screen conventions without interrupting the story’s momentum.

The diction alternates between polished, sometimes ceremonious narration and strongly colloquial speech. The narrative voice uses elaborate vocabulary—“ostentatiously,” “solicitude,” “misconstrued,” “systematic”—to frame childish behaviour with comic grandeur. William’s dialogue, by contrast, is rendered phonetically and idiomatically through forms such as “jus’,” “gotter,” “p’raps,” “kin’ly,” “pertic-ler” and “mornin’.” His speech is repetitive, argumentative and relentlessly explanatory. He rarely accepts correction; instead, he redefines events until he appears innocent or heroic. Adult dialogue is more standard but equally characterful. Mr Brown’s speech consists of explosions, rhetorical questions, repetitions and insults, while Mrs Brown’s mild, qualifying language acts as a domestic counterweight. Ethel and Mr Morgan speak in conventional polite formulas, and their awkward pauses turn social restraint into comedy.

Sentence rhythm varies according to the action. Long, cumulative sentences recreate the breathless excess of films, pursuits, emotional performances and parental complaints. Short sentences and fragments—particularly “Silence” and abrupt exchanges such as “Be quiet!”—control comic timing. Lists are another prominent device. William’s pocket contents, the stages of cinematic action and the father’s catalogue of offences all accumulate detail until the situation becomes ridiculous. Parenthetical qualifications and afterthoughts sharpen the narrator’s wit, while em dashes mark hesitation, interruption, melodramatic emphasis and sudden changes of direction.

Characterisation is achieved primarily through behaviour, speech and recurring verbal habits rather than psychological exposition. William is defined by his solemn concentration, physical appetite, literal imitation and capacity to convert scraps of observation into complete narratives. His imagination is theatrical: he changes his voice, posture and expression to suit each role, but he lacks the social knowledge needed to understand the original scenes. Mr Brown is characterised by bodily discomfort and verbal overreaction; his headache, digestion and injured dignity amplify every disturbance. Mrs Brown remains restrained and practical, while Joan’s credulity and Mr Morgan’s embarrassment allow William’s inventions to flourish.

Structurally, the story begins with a simple enabling incident—the gift of a shilling—then moves through purchase, cinema visit, imitation and domestic reckoning. The cinema programme functions as a set of motifs that are replayed in ordinary life: the crime film produces the chase home, the rustic romance shapes William’s exchange with Joan, the restrained lovers inspire his intervention with Mr Morgan, the painting comedy leads to the damaged door, and the temperance melodrama supplies the final vision of himself as a suffering child. This patterned recurrence gives the apparently episodic narrative strong unity. Transitions are smooth and often triggered by associative thought, so that one remembered image generates the next disaster.

The ending uses circularity and delayed recognition. William reviews the day as a series of noble acts unfairly misunderstood, just as his father reviews the same events as evidence of insanity. Neither possesses the whole explanation, although the reader does. William’s attempted deathbed-style forgiveness repeats the language of the final film and provides a last comic collision between melodrama and family reality. His decision to flee before finishing the line preserves his essential mixture of theatricality and practical instinct.

Overall, the style combines Edwardian or early twentieth-century domestic comedy, social observation, cinematic parody and child-centred farce. Its signature qualities are urbane narrative irony, affectionate treatment of mischief, formal prose set against colloquial dialogue, escalating misunderstandings, carefully timed repetition and a persistent contrast between William’s heroic self-conception and the mundane damage visible to everyone around him.

### WILLIAM AT THE PICTURES

William’s aunt gave him a shilling.

She did it at half-past ten on Saturday morning, when hope was still fresh and the day had not yet been spoiled by adults arranging it. She pressed the coin into his hand with the air of one rewarding virtue.

“There, William,” she said. “Spend it wisely.”

William promised that he would.

His conception of wisdom differed in certain details from his aunt’s, but this was hardly his fault. Adults spoke of spending wisely without ever defining the term. William, after grave consideration, decided that wisdom consisted in obtaining the greatest possible quantity of pleasure for the least possible quantity of money.

The cinema cost sixpence. That left sixpence for sweets.

The arrangement was perfect.

There were shops in the village where sixpence bought chocolates in a box adorned with a pink ribbon, and other shops where it bought eleven rather sad-looking caramels in a paper bag. William passed these without weakening. He went instead to a small, dark establishment whose window displayed bootlaces, postcards, paraffin, marbles, string, flypapers and sweets of a violent green colour. The proprietor had once objected when William counted the currants in a penny bun before buying it, but William had since forgiven him. Sixpence was too important to be influenced by private resentment.

“How many of those green ones d’you get for sixpence?” he demanded.

The proprietor looked at him without enthusiasm.

“A quarter of a pound.”

William leaned over the counter.

“They’ve been there a long time, haven’t they?”

“They have not.”

“They look as if they have.”

“Well, they haven’t.”

“P’raps they’re a bit stale.”

“They’re perfectly fresh.”

William sighed. Negotiations with unreasonable tradesmen were always exhausting.

“If they were stale,” he said patiently, “you’d give me more, wouldn’t you?”

“No.”

“Not even one more?”

“No.”

William examined the sweets. They were shaped like small cushions and covered with a fine white powder. Their greenness was not the greenness of grass or leaves, but a more ambitious greenness, suggesting that Nature had made an effort and failed.

“I’ll have sixpenn’orth,” he said at last, with the air of a financier concluding a doubtful but extensive transaction.

The bag made a gratifying bulge in his pocket. He ate three sweets on the way to the cinema and found them satisfactory. They adhered firmly to the teeth and possessed a flavour which, though not immediately recognisable, was powerful. William considered that delicacy of flavour was greatly overrated. What one wanted from a sweet was evidence that one had eaten it.

The afternoon performance had already begun when he entered. He crept down the darkened aisle, tripped over two pairs of feet, sat on a hat, apologised to the wrong person and finally settled himself in the front row.

On the screen a criminal was escaping from justice.

William recognised him as a criminal at once because he wore a cloth cap pulled over his eyes, kept looking behind him and carried a black bag which he ostentatiously concealed beneath his coat. These precautions were guaranteed to attract attention in any properly regulated street. A policeman appeared. The criminal ran. The policeman ran. Three more policemen joined them, followed by a man with a basket, a woman with a perambulator and a dog. The criminal climbed walls, fell through roofs, hid in barrels and emerged from chimneys. He had only to walk quietly into a shop and buy a collar to escape detection, but this did not occur to him. He preferred methods requiring courage, noise and a complete disregard for property.

William watched, spellbound.

Next came a romance of country life.

A simple country maiden lived with her old father in a cottage with roses round the door. She spent much of her time carrying a milk-pail which was always empty, possibly because a full one would have interfered with the more important business of emotion. A simple country son of the soil loved her. He wore gaiters, leaned upon gates and spoke in a husky voice. Unfortunately, a dark stranger also loved her. He could be identified as a villain by his moustache, which turned upwards at the ends and appeared to have independent designs upon the simple country maiden.

The maiden loved the simple country son of the soil but believed him faithless because she had seen him shaking hands with another woman. The son of the soil loved the maiden but believed her faithless because he had seen her accepting a letter from the postman. They therefore spent several reels avoiding each other behind haystacks. At last the dark stranger attempted to carry the maiden away in a motor-car. The son of the soil pursued on horseback, rescued her, injured his forehead slightly and married her.

William approved of the pursuit, though he thought the misunderstanding unnecessarily prolonged. He himself would have asked the postman what was in the letter.

There followed a comedy about a painter.

The painter had been ordered to paint a door. Instead, he painted his employer, the employer’s wife, a policeman, a cat and most of the street. At one point he removed old paint by holding a flame beneath it and scraping it off with a knife. This process particularly interested William. It was simple, scientific and produced a pleasing amount of smoke.

The final film was a drama against strong drink.

Its principal character was a drunkard with a white face and black hair. He had a small child whose duty it was to forgive him. The drunkard spent the housekeeping money, pawned the furniture, struck his employer, burned down his home and fell off a bridge. After each catastrophe the child clasped his hands and said, “Father, I forgive you.”

The child’s health was not good. He coughed whenever anyone entered the room and lay upon a narrow bed beneath a patchwork quilt. His forgiveness appeared to exhaust him so much that he repeatedly sank back upon the pillow with closed eyes, though he always recovered in time for the next offence.

At the end the drunkard knelt by the bed and promised to reform. The child raised one thin hand, smiled faintly and forgave him for the last time. The drunkard then became prosperous with remarkable speed, while the child, whose chief occupation was no longer required, died.

The lights went up.

William remained seated for a moment, blinking and thoughtful. He had passed through crime, love, art, intoxication, repentance and death in less than three hours. Ordinary village life seemed singularly empty by comparison.

Outside, the late afternoon was bright and peaceful. No criminals fled over the roofs. No maidens were being carried away. No fathers reeled from public houses to receive the forgiveness of dying children. Mr Bott’s dog slept in the road.

William put a green sweet into his mouth and started home.

At the corner by the church he remembered the criminal film.

At once the street altered. The hedge became the wall of a prison, the vicarage a den of spies and the elderly lady approaching with a basket a detective in disguise. William drew his cap over his eyes, thrust the bag of sweets inside his jersey and glanced furtively behind him.

The elderly lady moved aside.

William increased his speed.

He could hear the police gaining upon him. They were silent police, which made them more dangerous. One was creeping along the ditch. Another had climbed the telegraph pole. A third was disguised as Mr Bott’s dog.

William broke into a run.

He dashed through his own gate, sprang across the lawn, rounded a laurel bush and collided with his father.

Mr Brown had been enjoying ten minutes of quiet before dinner. He was seated in a deck-chair with the newspaper spread before him and a cup of tea balanced upon one knee. William’s arrival sent the tea over his waistcoat, the newspaper over his head and the deck-chair backwards into a flower-bed.

There was a brief interval during which Mr Brown’s legs, the newspaper and the deck-chair struggled for supremacy. Then his face appeared.

“William!”

William looked round quickly. The imaginary police had vanished at the first sign of trouble, as imaginary police often did.

“Yes, Father?”

“What do you mean by it?”

“I was only comin’ home.”

“Coming home? Coming home? Do you generally come home like a battering-ram?”

“I was being chased.”

“Chased? Who was chasing you?”

William glanced towards the gate. It was empty.

“Some men,” he said.

“What men?”

“I don’t know their names.”

Mr Brown rose. Tea dripped from his waistcoat. Earth adhered to his trousers. His expression suggested that William’s ignorance of the men’s names was the least unsatisfactory feature of the affair.

“What’s that in your jersey?”

“Nothin’.”

“It’s not nothing. Give it to me.”

William reluctantly produced the bag. Mr Brown seized it.

“Sweets! Of course! Stuffing yourself with this poisonous rubbish and charging about like a lunatic! Here!”

He flung the bag over the hedge into the kitchen garden.

William watched its flight with horror.

“You needn’t’ve done that,” he said.

“You needn’t have knocked me into the flower-bed!”

“I didn’t knock you. I jus’ happened to be runnin’ where you happened to be sittin’.”

“Go indoors!”

William went round the house instead.

The bag had burst upon landing. Green sweets lay among the cabbages, on the path and in a bed recently dressed with soot. William collected them with anxious devotion. A smaller-minded person might have rejected those which had fallen into the soil. William merely rubbed them upon his sleeve. By the end of the operation he had consumed sweets and garden in approximately equal quantities.

He had just secured the last when Joan appeared at the fence next door.

Joan was eight and possessed the valuable quality of believing most things until someone older contradicted them.

“What are you doing?” she asked.

William straightened slowly.

The romance returned to him. He was no longer a boy kneeling among cabbages with a torn bag. He was a simple country son of the soil, weather-beaten by sorrow, silent beneath injustice and probably leaning upon a gate. As no gate stood conveniently near, he leaned upon a rake.

“Nothin’,” he said huskily.

Joan stared.

“What’s the matter with your voice?”

William gazed into the distance. The simple country son of the soil had always gazed into the distance before speaking. It gave significance to even the most ordinary remark.

“It’s always like this,” he said in a deep whisper.

“No, it isn’t.”

“It is now.”

“Have you got a cold?”

William considered the question. A cold was not romantic. Weak lungs were romantic. He remembered the drunkard’s child, coughing delicately upon the patchwork quilt.

“It’s my lungs,” he said.

Joan’s eyes widened.

“What’s wrong with them?”

“They’re weak.”

“Are you going to die?”

William had not intended to go as far as death, but Joan’s awed expression encouraged him.

“P’raps,” he said. “The doctor says I’ve gotter be careful.”

“What doctor?”

“A special one.”

Joan came nearer to the fence.

“You don’t look ill.”

“People with weak lungs don’t,” said William. “Not till the end.”

He coughed. His first attempt sounded more like a bark, but the second was softer and more affecting.

Joan was impressed.

“You ought to go to bed.”

“I can’t. I’ve got things to do first.”

“What things?”

William had not prepared the details.

“Important things,” he said.

He drew out the remains of the bag.

“Like to have a sweet?”

Joan hesitated.

“They’re dirty.”

“They’re not dirty. That’s medicine powder on them.”

“They’ve got earth on them.”

“Earth’s good for you. Potatoes grow in it.”

The argument was unanswerable. Joan accepted one.

The sweet required energetic attention. When she had subdued it she accepted another, then another. William, taking his duties as host seriously, selected those least heavily coated with soot. Their flavour had broadened since the purchase and now included cabbage, leather and the kitchen garden generally.

Joan ate five.

William ate seven.

Then Joan said that she felt funny.

“That’s because you’re not used to medicine powder,” said William.

“I think I’m going to be sick.”

“Don’t be silly. People in pictures never are.”

Joan turned pale and went home hurriedly.

William remained by the rake, coughing from time to time and staring across the cabbages. There was no simple country maiden present to overhear him, and the effect was therefore wasted. After a few minutes he abandoned the role.

At dinner that evening Mrs Brown said, “William, Mrs Clive has just telephoned.”

William continued to eat.

“She says Joan has been very sick.”

“Has she?” said William politely.

“She says you gave her some sweets covered with dirt.”

“They weren’t covered with dirt.”

“What were they covered with?”

“Only bits of it.”

Mr Brown lowered his fork.

“Are these the sweets I threw away?”

“I didn’t throw them away,” said William. “You did.”

“Did you pick them up?”

“Well, I wasn’t goin’ to waste them.”

“And then you gave them to that child?”

“I gave her the cleanest ones.”

Mr Brown closed his eyes. He had recovered from the tea, but not from the memory of it.

Mrs Brown said mildly, “Mrs Clive also says that Joan is terribly upset because you told her you were dying of weak lungs.”

Ethel looked up. Ethel was William’s elder sister and had reached an age at which William’s mere presence seemed to her an offence against civilisation.

“Dying?” she said. “What nonsense!”

“I didn’t say I was dying,” said William. “I only said p’raps I was.”

“Why?”

“She asked me.”

“You made your voice sound ill,” said Mrs Brown.

“I can’t help my voice.”

“Your voice sounds perfectly normal now.”

“It comes and goes.”

Mr Brown opened his eyes.

“If it doesn’t go,” he said, “you will.”

William judged it prudent to finish dinner in silence.

Afterwards he passed the drawing-room and heard Ethel speaking to Jack Morgan near the open window. Jack Morgan was a young man who came to the house rather often, though never, so far as William could see, for any useful purpose. He played tennis badly, drank tea slowly and spent a great deal of time telling Ethel things that did not appear to interest either of them.

“I suppose,” Ethel was saying, “you’ll be seeing quite a lot of Margaret at the Harrisons’.”

“Possibly,” said Jack.

“Of course, it’s nothing to me.”

“No,” said Jack. “And I suppose you’ll be seeing young Fenton?”

“Perhaps.”

“Of course, it’s nothing to me.”

“No.”

There was a silence of immense emotional depth.

William stopped beneath the window.

Here, unmistakably, were the lovers from the picture. They loved each other, but pride held them apart. Ethel was the simple country maiden, though the description required some generosity, and Jack was the simple country son of the soil, though he wore no gaiters and worked in a bank. Margaret and young Fenton were obstacles placed in their path by Fate. Unless someone intervened, Ethel would carry empty milk-pails about for several reels and Jack would lean bitterly upon gates.

William entered the room.

“Go away, William,” said Ethel.

He studied them compassionately.

“You oughtn’t to let pride come between you,” he said.

Ethel flushed.

“What on earth do you mean?”

“Nothin’,” said William, with tact, and withdrew.

The matter occupied him deeply. In the film, the lovers had waited until the villain’s motor-car forced a decision. William saw no reason to wait. He possessed information, courage and most of the remaining evening.

He went into the garden and looked for a flower suitable for conveying Ethel’s emotions. The roses were nearly over. He found a small pink bud, slightly damaged by rain, and pulled it from the bush. On the way to Jack’s house he carried it in his pocket with a penknife, two marbles, string, a piece of chalk and half a biscuit. By the time he arrived, it had lost its petals and acquired a coating of biscuit crumbs. Nevertheless, its symbolism remained.

Jack himself opened the door.

“Hullo, William,” he said cautiously.

“I’ve brought you a message from Ethel.”

Jack’s caution increased.

“What message?”

William held out the crushed rosebud.

“She sent you this.”

Jack took it.

“Did she?”

“Yes. She picked it with tears in her eyes.”

Jack examined the object, perhaps in search of the tears.

“What did she say?”

“She said, ‘Take this to him, William, and tell him I’m wastin’ away.’”

“Did she really?”

“Yes,” said William. “She can’t eat.”

Jack looked surprised.

“She ate a fairly substantial tea.”

“She was pretendin’. She does that so people won’t know.”

“I see.”

“She walks about all night callin’ your name.”

“Does she?”

“Not loud,” William added. “You wouldn’t hear her from here.”

Jack’s mouth twitched, but William was too occupied with tragedy to notice.

“She wants to meet you secret,” he continued. “At seven.”

“Where?”

“At our house.”

“That isn’t especially secret.”

“It is if you don’t tell anyone.”

“What am I to say when I arrive?”

“Say you’ve come to see Father. Then when no one’s lookin’ you can tell Ethel you forgive her.”

“For what?”

William frowned. Jack was taking a narrow view.

“For Margaret and young Fenton and pride an’ all that.”

“Ah,” said Jack. “Naturally.”

“You’ll come?”

“I shouldn’t miss it.”

William returned home with the satisfaction of one who has reunited two lives. He did not mention his success. Great benefactors are often silent.

At seven o’clock the Brown family was at dinner.

Mr Brown had reached a condition of comparative peace. Joan’s illness had been reported as temporary, William had said nothing for nearly an hour, and the soup was hot. Then the bell rang.

The maid entered.

“Mr Morgan, sir.”

Ethel dropped her spoon.

Mr Brown stared.

“At this hour?”

Jack appeared in the doorway, carrying the remains of the rosebud.

“I’m terribly sorry,” he began. “I hope I’m not interrupting.”

“You are,” said Mr Brown.

Mrs Brown intervened.

“Do come in, Jack. Is anything the matter?”

Jack looked at Ethel. Ethel looked at the rose. The rose, though much the worse for experience, pointed unmistakably towards William.

“I received a message,” said Jack.

“What message?” demanded Ethel.

Jack held out the flower.

“This.”

Ethel’s face became scarlet.

William watched with pleased expectancy. In the picture, this was the moment when the maiden placed both hands upon her heart.

“I never sent that!” said Ethel.

“You did,” said William helpfully. “You picked it with tears in your eyes.”

“I did nothing of the kind!”

“You said you were wastin’ away.”

“William!”

“You said you couldn’t eat.”

Ethel turned to Jack.

“I haven’t the faintest idea what he means.”

Jack’s expression was courteous but unsteady.

“He also mentioned that you walk about at night calling my name.”

Mr Brown rose slowly.

“William,” he said, “have you been interfering again?”

“I haven’t interfered. I was helpin’.”

“Helping whom?”

“Them. They’re in love with each other, but they’re too proud to say so.”

Silence.

It was not an ordinary silence. It was a silence composed of Mr Brown’s fury, Mrs Brown’s embarrassment, Ethel’s mortification, Jack’s suppressed amusement and William’s dawning suspicion that romantic assistance was not appreciated in private life.

Ethel spoke first.

“I hate you!”

“That’s what the girl said in the picture,” William replied eagerly. “But she didn’t really. She—”

“Be quiet!” roared Mr Brown.

Jack placed the rosebud carefully beside his plate.

“Perhaps,” he said, “I had better go.”

“Yes,” said Ethel.

“No,” said Mrs Brown at the same moment. “Do stay and have some dinner.”

“I think perhaps—another time.”

He left amid polite phrases from Mrs Brown, an icy stare from Ethel and a sound from Mr Brown resembling the preliminary disturbance of a volcano.

William was sent upstairs.

He went unwillingly. His behaviour, he felt, had been systematically misconstrued. He had rescued invisible pursuers from the trouble of catching him, recovered valuable property, shared it generously with Joan, faced death without complaint and united two lovers. For these achievements he had been shouted at, accused and deprived of pudding.

His room offered no comfort. It contained no secret passage, no rustic maiden and no patchwork quilt. The door, however, was painted.

William remembered the painter.

Here at last was an occupation beyond emotional misunderstanding. It was practical, scientific and useful. The paint on his door was chipped near the handle. He would remove the old paint and perhaps, if time allowed, repaint it. His father could hardly object to an improvement of property.

William found a candle and his penknife. He lit the candle, held it near the lower panel and scraped. Nothing happened. He moved the flame closer. The paint softened, blistered and turned brown. A gratifying smell filled the room.

He scraped harder.

Long curls came away. Beneath them appeared bare wood, blackened in places but undeniably clean. Encouraged, William extended the operation. The painter in the film had worked quickly, with broad gestures and no concern for straight lines. William did the same.

Soon the lower half of the door presented a varied surface of scorched wood, hanging strips, knife marks and islands of untouched paint. Smoke drifted into the passage.

Mr Brown came upstairs.

He opened the door, saw William kneeling with candle and knife, and remained perfectly still.

This stillness was more alarming than speech.

“What,” he said at last, “are you doing?”

“Strippin’ paint.”

“Stripping paint.”

“Yes. It’s a new way. You use fire.”

Mr Brown looked at the door.

“You’ve burned it.”

“I haven’t burned all of it.”

“You’ve ruined it!”

“I was improvin’ it.”

“With a candle?”

“The man in the picture did.”

Mr Brown seized the candle and blew it out.

“Pictures! Is that what’s been the matter with you? Charging into me, poisoning the child next door, telling people you’re dying, making a fool of Ethel, dragging Morgan here in the middle of dinner, and now setting fire to the house!”

“I didn’t set fire to the house.”

“You were trying to!”

“I wasn’t. I was only takin’ the paint off.”

“You are insane,” said Mr Brown. “Completely insane. No sane human being could produce this amount of destruction in one day.”

William stood with injured dignity.

“I was only tryin’ to help.”

“Help! Help! You nearly break my neck and call it help. You feed filthy sweets to Joan and call it help. You meddle in your sister’s affairs and call it help. You destroy a door and call it help. I suppose if you blew up the house you’d expect me to thank you!”

“No,” said William reasonably. “Not if you were in it.”

Mr Brown made a brief but impressive speech upon obedience, truthfulness, property, fire, sweets, sisters, neighbours, cinemas, insanity and the probable future of boys who persisted in behaving like William. He then imposed a punishment of such magnitude that William ceased to follow its details after the first fortnight.

When Mr Brown had gone, William sat on the bed.

His life was tragic.

He had been misunderstood by everyone. Even the drunkard’s child had not suffered so persistently, though admittedly he had possessed a more satisfactory cough. William recalled the child’s pale face, thin hand and inexhaustible forgiveness. At once his own course became clear. He would forgive his father. Not angrily or ostentatiously, but quietly, as one standing upon the edge of another world.

He descended the stairs.

Mr Brown was in the hall, telling Mrs Brown about the door.

“Burned it!” he was saying. “Actually burned it! If I hadn’t gone up, the whole place might have been in flames. The boy’s a menace. A public menace!”

William appeared on the bottom step. He leaned against the banister and coughed faintly.

No one noticed.

He coughed again.

Mr Brown turned.

“What do you want?”

William raised one hand. He had intended it to tremble, but the effort made it wave instead.

“Father,” he said huskily, “I forgive you.”

Mr Brown stared.

“You what?”

“I forgive you for all you’ve done to me.”

“What I’ve done to you!”

“When I’m gone,” continued William, “you’ll remember my last words. You’ll come to my little bed an’ say, ‘William, can you forgive me?’ An’ I’ll smile faintly an’ say—”

Mr Brown advanced.

The drunkard in the film had fallen upon his knees at this point. Mr Brown showed no intention of doing so. His movements suggested an entirely different ending.

William’s dramatic instinct yielded promptly to his practical one.

He sprang through the open front door, raced down the path and disappeared into the gathering dusk before forgiveness could be completed.

Behind him came his father’s voice.

Ahead lay the road, the hedge, the darkening fields and all the inexhaustible possibilities of another pursuit.

William drew his cap over his eyes and ran.

### The Cartographer of Lost Roads

Every morning, before the city woke, Mara Venn unfolded a map that did not exist.

It covered the largest table in the Department of Civic Memory, though the table was twelve feet long and made from a single slab of black oak. The map was thin as onion skin and pale as winter breath. Streets ran across it in faded blue veins, splitting and rejoining beneath Mara’s fingertips. Some were roads everyone knew: Bellmaker Avenue, Orchard Row, the Nine Bridges. Others appeared only at dawn and vanished when the bells struck eight.

Those were the roads Mara was employed to erase.

“Unlicensed geography,” Director Vale called them.

The Department had been founded after the Great Revision, when the city council decided that too many streets, alleys, staircases, tunnels, and unofficial courtyards made the capital difficult to govern. A place could not be taxed if it shifted overnight. It could not be policed if doors opened onto different neighborhoods each Tuesday. It could not be trusted if citizens sometimes walked home by routes their grandparents remembered but no modern survey recorded.

So the Department simplified the city.

Its cartographers wore gray coats and carried silver knives. When a lost road appeared on the dawn map, one of them was sent to find its entrance and cut the road from the city’s memory.

Mara had been doing this for eleven years.

She was very good at it.

At twenty minutes past six on a rainy autumn morning, she found a new line on the map.

It began behind the Central Railway Station, crossed beneath buildings that had no tunnels, curved through the sealed gardens of the old palace, and ended at a small square drawn in gold ink. At the center of the square stood a symbol Mara had never seen before: a circle enclosing a tiny door.

Beside it, in handwriting she recognized, were four words:

COME BEFORE THEY FORGET.

Mara stared at the message until the rain began tapping harder against the high windows.

The handwriting belonged to her brother.

Elias had been missing for seventeen years.

She was still looking at the words when Director Vale entered the map room.

He was a narrow man with colorless hair and a face that always seemed reflected in cold glass. He wore no cartographer’s knife. Directors did not cut roads themselves. They sent others, then signed the documents proving the roads had never existed.

“You’re early,” he said.

“So are you.”

“I don’t sleep much.”

“Neither do guilty men.”

For a moment, his expression sharpened. Then he smiled.

“You’ve found something.”

Mara placed both hands on the map, covering the golden square and her brother’s message. “A service lane near the eastern warehouses.”

“Unusual?”

“No.”

Vale approached the table. “Then why are you hiding it?”

Mara met his eyes. Lying to the Department was dangerous. Lying over an active map was worse. Maps listened. That was why cartographers were trained never to speak of routes they wished to conceal.

“I spilled tea,” she said. “The stain is embarrassing.”

Vale looked at the dry table, at the empty cup near Mara’s elbow, and then at her face.

The clock on the wall ticked six thirty.

Finally, he stepped back.

“Erase whatever you found before eight,” he said. “The council is inspecting the Department today. We must not appear untidy.”

When he left, Mara waited until his footsteps disappeared down the marble corridor. Then she copied the route onto the inside of her left wrist. The ink trembled slightly as she traced the final turn.

At seven, she took her coat, her knife, and a spool of red thread. By seven fifteen, she stood behind the Central Railway Station, facing a brick wall slick with rain.

According to every official map, the wall separated the station from a printing house. According to the dawn map, an entrance should have been there.

Mara placed her palm against the bricks.

“Elias,” she whispered.

Nothing happened.

She tried the old rhyme he had taught her when they were children:

“A road remembered, a road revealed.
A name unspoken, a doorway unsealed.”

The bricks sighed.

A narrow archway appeared, filled with darkness.

Mara tied one end of the red thread to a drainpipe. Lost roads rarely permitted travelers to return the same way they entered, but thread possessed a memory of its own. That was why old stories were full of spindles, knots, woven paths, and women who knew how to follow them.

She stepped through the arch.

Behind the wall lay a lane bright with afternoon sunlight.

Mara turned in surprise. The archway had vanished. Her red thread continued into a smooth stone wall.

The lane sloped gently downward between leaning houses painted green and yellow. Laundry fluttered from balconies. Somewhere, a violin played the same six notes again and again. The air smelled of bread, coal smoke, and summer dust.

Mara knew this place.

Not from life, but from a photograph.

Her mother had once shown her a picture of a narrow lane where she and Elias had been born. The official records said the neighborhood had been demolished before Mara’s birth, yet here it stood, warmed by a sun that did not belong to the rainy morning outside.

An old woman sat beneath a striped awning, peeling apples.

“You’re late,” she said.

“For what?”

“For almost everything.”

Mara approached carefully. “What is this road called?”

The woman laughed. “You have a silver knife and ask a road its name? That is like carrying an ax into a forest and asking the trees for directions.”

Mara kept her hand away from the knife at her belt. “I’m not here to erase anything.”

“Aren’t you?”

“No.”

The old woman cut a long spiral of apple skin. It fell unbroken into her lap.

“You’ve erased two hundred and thirteen roads, Mara Venn.”

The number struck her like a slap. “How do you know my name?”

“We keep count.”

“Who are you?”

“Someone you made homeless.”

The woman nodded toward the nearest doorway. Its green paint was blistered, and a brass plate hung beside it.

I. SORREL, SEAMSTRESS.

Mara remembered Sorrel Passage. She had erased it nine years ago after residents reported hearing dead relatives singing beneath the pavement. The assignment had taken less than an hour. One cut across the alley’s nameplate, one cut through the municipal map, and the passage had folded itself into mist.

Officially, no one had lived there.

Mara looked again at the woman.

“I didn’t know.”

“No,” said Irena Sorrel. “You were paid not to.”

The violin stopped.

All along the lane, windows opened. Faces appeared: men, women, children, some dressed in current fashions, others in clothes from decades earlier. They watched Mara without speaking.

She felt the weight of the silver knife.

“Where is my brother?” she asked.

Irena pointed downhill. “At the end, if the road still likes you.”

Mara followed the lane.

It changed as she walked. Painted houses became warehouses, then gardens, then rows of tiny shops. She passed a courtyard full of white chickens and recognized it as Feather Court, erased during her first year at the Department. She crossed a bridge she had cut from memory because it appeared only during storms. Beneath it flowed a black river carrying paper boats.

Each boat bore a name.

Some names were written in careful ink. Others in crayon. Thousands passed under the bridge, vanishing into darkness.

“What are those?” Mara asked a boy leaning over the railing.

“People no one remembers,” he said.

“Are they dead?”

“Not always.”

Beyond the bridge, the road narrowed into steps. At the top stood the sealed gardens of the old palace.

Mara had seen them only from outside. Their iron gates had been locked for seventy years, since the last queen left the city. Yet inside this hidden geography, the gardens were alive. Red flowers climbed broken statues. Pear trees bent beneath silver fruit. Fountains whispered into mossy basins.

A man waited beside a dry reflecting pool.

He was older than the brother Mara remembered. Of course he was. Elias had vanished at nineteen; he would be thirty-six now. There was gray at his temples, and a scar crossed his chin. But he still stood with his hands in his pockets, shoulders slightly hunched, as if apologizing for being taller than everyone around him.

Mara stopped.

He smiled.

“Hello, little bird.”

No one else had called her that.

She crossed the distance between them and struck him hard across the face.

Elias stumbled, more surprised than hurt.

“You left me,” she said.

“I know.”

“You were alive.”

“Yes.”

“For seventeen years.”

“Yes.”

She struck him again, then pulled him into an embrace so fierce they both nearly fell into the empty pool.

Elias held her while she wept.

At last, Mara stepped back. “Why didn’t you come home?”

“I tried.”

“You could have sent word.”

“I tried that too.”

“The message on the map—”

“Took me seventeen years.”

He sat on the edge of the pool and motioned for her to join him.

“When I disappeared, I was working as a courier,” he said. “One night I took a shortcut through Lantern Alley. The Department erased it while I was inside.”

Mara remembered the alley. Not the assignment, but the history. Lantern Alley had been among the first roads removed after the Great Revision.

“What happened?”

“I came out here. The refuge.”

She looked around the garden. “This place contains erased roads.”

“Not just roads. Everything connected to them. Houses. shops. sometimes people. Whatever the official city refuses to remember ends up here.”

“Why couldn’t you leave?”

“Exits are difficult. The refuge is made from interrupted journeys. It knows how to take people in, not how to let them go.”

Mara thought of the red thread trailing behind her. When she checked her wrist, she saw that the spool was almost empty.

“Then how do I get back?”

“You may not.”

She stood. “You called me here without knowing if I could return?”

“I called you because the refuge is dying.”

As if in answer, a tremor passed through the garden. Leaves shivered. One of the pear trees became transparent, then solid again.

Elias reached into his coat and removed a folded map. Unlike the Department’s pale dawn map, this one was patched from hundreds of materials: paper, cloth, bark, ticket stubs, letters, scraps of wallpaper. Roads had been sewn onto it with dark thread.

“At first, erased places survived because people remembered them,” he said. “A shop remained as long as someone recalled buying bread there. A staircase endured because an old woman dreamed of climbing it as a girl. But the Department became more efficient. It didn’t just remove roads from maps. It removed records, photographs, stories.”

Mara looked at the stitched map. Sections along its edges were unraveling.

“When memory dies outside,” Elias said, “the refuge dies inside. Three streets vanished last week. There were people on them.”

“Where did they go?”

“No one knows.”

Another tremor shook the garden. This time, a statue cracked.

“What do you need me to do?”

“Stop the Department.”

She laughed once, without humor. “There are forty cartographers. Archives beneath three ministries. Guards, clerks, councilors—”

“And one original map.”

Mara fell silent.

Every map used by the Department was copied from an older master survey, kept in the director’s private vault. Rumor said the master map showed not only the city as it was, but every version of the city that had ever existed. It was the source of the Department’s authority. A road cut from the master map disappeared from public memory.

“If the roads were restored to the original,” Elias continued, “people might remember.”

“Might?”

“That is the best promise any map can make.”

A bell rang in the distance.

Seven thirty.

The sound crossed impossible streets from the official city. Mara had thirty minutes before the dawn map faded and the golden route disappeared.

“The council is inspecting the Department today,” she said slowly.

“Then everyone who built this machine will be in one place.”

Mara looked at her brother. “Can you find a way out?”

Elias smiled and pointed to the spool at her belt.

Only six inches of red thread remained.

“The road still likes you,” he said.

They ran.

The refuge rearranged itself around them. Gardens folded into courtyards. Bridges rose like drawstrings. Streets curled through markets and vanished behind closing doors. Residents watched from windows as Mara and Elias followed the thread.

At the end, they found Irena Sorrel waiting beside the stone wall.

“You came here as a cartographer,” she told Mara. “How will you leave?”

Mara removed the silver knife from her belt.

She had received it at twenty-one, along with her gray coat and her oath. The blade was engraved with the Department’s motto:

ORDER IS MERCY.

She remembered all the roads she had cut. Two hundred and thirteen. She remembered how cleanly they had disappeared.

Mara snapped the knife against the wall.

The blade broke in two.

“Without a profession,” she said.

Irena smiled and pulled the red thread.

The wall opened.

Rain struck Mara’s face. She fell into the alley behind the station, Elias tumbling after her. The archway sealed at once.

For several seconds, he lay on the wet pavement laughing.

“What?” Mara asked.

“I haven’t felt rain in seventeen years.”

She pulled him to his feet. “Enjoy it while running.”

They reached the Department at seven forty-five.

Council carriages lined the street. Guards clustered beneath black umbrellas. Inside, clerks hurried through corridors carrying boxes of records meant to impress inspectors with their weight and uselessness.

Mara and Elias entered through the eastern archive door. She led him down a servants’ stair, past the room where condemned street signs were burned, and into the basement.

The director’s vault stood behind three iron doors.

Mara knew the first combination because all senior cartographers knew it. Elias picked the second lock with a piece of wire. The third door had neither lock nor handle, only a blank brass plate.

“It opens to a forgotten name,” Mara said.

“Whose?”

“Vale’s, I think.”

“His first name?”

“No one knows it.”

Footsteps sounded on the stairs.

Mara examined the brass plate. Directors of Civic Memory surrendered their given names upon appointment. The symbolic sacrifice supposedly allowed them to act without personal bias. Their names were removed from certificates, family records, and public documents.

But maps remembered what people did not.

Mara took out the broken half of her knife and cut her palm. She pressed the bloodied blade against the plate.

“Show me the road to the man he was.”

Lines appeared in the brass: a house, a garden, a child standing beside a gate. Beneath them, one word emerged.

THOMAS.

Mara spoke it aloud.

The door opened.

Director Vale stood on the other side.

He wore his formal white coat, and in his hand was a pistol.

“I hoped you would disappoint me less dramatically,” he said.

Elias moved in front of Mara.

Vale aimed at his chest. “You should be grateful, Mr. Venn. Your disappearance gave your sister purpose.”

“You knew where he was,” Mara said.

“I suspected.”

“All these years?”

“The Department has always known that erasure leaves residue. It is unfortunate but necessary.”

“People live there.”

“People live everywhere. That does not make everywhere useful.”

Behind him, the master map hung from ceiling to floor.

It was enormous, far larger than Mara had imagined. The city covered it in layers of ink: black streets over red streets, blue rivers beneath gold districts, erased neighborhoods shining faintly like bones under skin.

Several councilors stood around it. Their expressions ranged from outrage to fear. Director Vale had clearly interrupted their inspection to deal with the intrusion.

Mara raised her bleeding hand.

“You told them there was no refuge, didn’t you?”

Vale’s eyes narrowed.

One councilor, a heavy woman wearing the chain of the western district, looked from Mara to Elias. “Who is this man?”

“Someone the Department erased,” Mara said.

“An agitator,” Vale replied. “Nothing more.”

“My name is Elias Venn. I was born in Candle Lane. I worked for the city courier service. I disappeared on the sixth of March, seventeen years ago, when Lantern Alley was removed.”

The councilor frowned. “I remember Lantern Alley.”

Vale turned toward her. “You do not.”

“I bought a blue lamp there when I was first married.”

A golden line flickered on the master map.

Everyone saw it.

Vale fired.

The shot struck Elias in the shoulder and spun him to the floor. Mara lunged forward before Vale could aim again. She drove the broken cartographer’s knife through his white sleeve and pinned his arm to the wooden map frame.

He screamed and dropped the pistol.

Guards rushed into the vault, but the councilor with the chain raised one hand.

“Wait.”

The golden line on the map was growing.

“Say it again,” Mara told her.

“Lantern Alley,” the woman whispered. “There was a lamp shop on the corner. The owner had yellow teeth. My husband said the lamps were overpriced.”

Buildings appeared along the line.

Another councilor stepped closer to the map. “My father took me to a dentist in Feather Court.”

A courtyard bloomed in red ink.

A guard lowered his sword. “There was a bridge near the southern mills. Only showed up when it rained.”

Blue ink curved across the river.

Names filled the vault.

Clerks gathered at the doors, then servants, guards, inspectors. Someone remembered a bakery beneath the palace wall. Someone else recalled a staircase that led to the theater balcony. A woman began singing a rhyme about Orchard Steps, and three others joined her.

With every memory, the master map changed.

Vale tore his sleeve free and reached for the pistol. Elias, pale and bleeding, kicked it under the table.

“You fools,” Vale shouted. “Do you know what the city was before us? Doors led into strangers’ dreams. Roads changed direction at night. Whole districts celebrated laws of their own invention. We created order!”

“You created absence,” Mara said.

“We created mercy!”

“No. You made the city easier to rule and harder to love.”

The clock upstairs began striking eight.

The dawn map would be fading. The golden route to the refuge would disappear. Mara watched the master map tremble as hundreds of hidden lines fought to return.

It was not enough.

Memory had opened the roads, but something still held them back. Every restored line stopped at the map’s edge, unable to cross into the physical city.

Elias gripped his wounded shoulder. “The cuts,” he said.

Mara understood.

For decades, cartographers had sliced roads from the master map. The cuts had healed into thin scars, sealing lost places away.

They needed to be reopened.

Mara pulled the broken knife from Vale’s sleeve.

Then she slashed the master map from top to bottom.

The councilors cried out. Vale made a sound like a dying animal.

For one breath, nothing happened.

Then the city remembered.

The vault walls vanished behind a flood of sunlight. A summer lane crossed the basement, carrying painted houses with it. Irena Sorrel sat beneath her awning, still peeling the same apple. The black river poured through the archive without wetting a single page. Bridges unfolded through ministry offices. Gardens erupted from stone corridors. Trees broke through the roof in showers of red tile.

All across the capital, forgotten doors opened.

A staircase appeared in the central courthouse and climbed toward a neighborhood absent for fifty years. Lantern Alley returned between a bank and a prison, every lamp in its windows burning blue. In the western district, three demolished courtyards unfolded inside one another like paper flowers.

People emerged slowly.

Some found relatives waiting, older than when they had last seen them. Others found no one, but stood in the streets speaking their names to anyone who would listen.

The city groaned under the weight of its own history.

Then it expanded.

Walls shifted outward. The river bent. Towers moved aside to make room for vanished houses. Roads crossed in impossible ways, yet no buildings fell. The capital did not return to what it had been. It became every version of itself at once.

Director Vale stood amid the transformation, staring at the name still faintly visible on the brass door.

Thomas.

A white-haired man in a gardener’s coat had appeared on the summer lane. He looked at Vale for a long time.

“Tom?” he said.

Vale collapsed to his knees.

Mara turned away.

Elias was sitting against the map table, blood soaking his coat. She knelt beside him and pressed both hands to the wound.

“You came back,” she said. “You are not allowed to die now.”

“That sounds like an official regulation.”

“It is.”

He smiled weakly. “Then I suppose I’d better comply.”

Help came from a hospital that had been erased thirty years earlier. Its doctors carried Elias across the black river to a bright green ward where old medicine and new medicine had learned, within minutes, to cooperate.

He survived.

In the months that followed, the Department of Civic Memory was dissolved. Its records were opened, its knives melted down, and its headquarters converted into a public station for travelers who became lost on roads that existed only on certain days.

Mara refused every official position offered to her.

Instead, she opened a small map shop in Candle Lane, beside Irena Sorrel’s new dressmaking room. Elias lived upstairs and complained about the stairs, though he climbed them easily.

The city remained difficult.

Commuters sometimes arrived at work yesterday. Children took shortcuts through royal gardens and came home speaking obsolete dialects. Tax collectors protested that several houses existed in more than one district. The council spent years debating whether a bridge that appeared only during storms required year-round maintenance.

But people adapted.

They carried thread. They learned the names of their neighbors. They told stories about the places they loved, understanding at last that memory was not a private luxury but a form of architecture.

Each morning, before the city woke, Mara unfolded a new map across her worktable.

It was never the same map twice.

She did not erase the roads that appeared and vanished. She marked them carefully, adding notes for travelers.

THIS WAY IS SAFE IF YOU ARE SINGING.

DO NOT ENTER AFTER THE THIRD BELL.

LEADS HOME, BUT NOT NECESSARILY YOURS.

And sometimes, beside a road drawn in gold ink, she wrote:

COME BEFORE THEY FORGET.
